question.text: A corporate treasurer needs to lock in a maximum borrowing cost for a future loan but also wants to benefit if rates decline. Which instrument best meets this requirement?

answer.text: Buy an interest rate cap (series of call options on interest rates) to limit the maximum rate while retaining downside benefit
Enter an interest rate futures contract to fix the rate completely
Sell interest rate put options to generate premium income
Enter an interest rate swap to exchange floating for fixed rate

explanation.text: The Logic: An interest rate cap — conceptually a strip of call options on the reference rate, one per reset period — pays off whenever the rate sets above the strike, capping the effective borrowing cost at that strike plus the upfront premium. Because the cap holder is only long options, the borrower benefits fully if rates instead fall: the caplets simply expire worthless and the loan resets at the lower market rate. This combination of a ceiling with retained downside benefit is what the treasurer needs. The Trap: An interest rate futures contract locks in the rate symmetrically, removing the downside benefit if rates fall. An interest rate swap (floating-to-fixed) similarly fixes the cost and eliminates the upside. Selling interest-rate puts generates premium but does not cap the borrowing cost on the upside and adds exposure if rates fall sharply. Note: The cited workbook (NISM Series IV, pages 21, 142, 154, 165) covers Floating Rate Bond caps capping issuer obligations, Black-model pricing for caps/floors, OTC IRO products including caps/floors, and futures locking in borrowing cost — but does not explicitly describe a cap as a strip of calls used by a borrower to limit maximum cost while retaining downside benefit. The framing above is standard interest-rate-derivatives knowledge.
